US states by general coastline (NOAA).New Hampshire: New Hampshire has the shortest coast of any coastal state, yet Hampton Beach draws huge summer crowds.
US states by general coastline (NOAA).Delaware: Delaware was the first state to ratify the US Constitution, in 1787, earning it the nickname 'the First State'.
US states by general coastline (NOAA).Georgia: Georgia's coast has barrier islands, and wild horses roam Cumberland Island, its largest and wildest.
US states by general coastline (NOAA).Washington: Washington's tidal shoreline, counting Puget Sound's countless inlets, is vastly longer than this general coastline figure suggests.
US states by general coastline (NOAA).North Carolina: Its Outer Banks are home to the Wright brothers' first flight at Kitty Hawk and the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse, the tallest brick lighthouse in the US.
US states by general coastline (NOAA).Louisiana: The state has lost nearly 2,000 square miles of coastal land since the 1930s, as sinking, erosion and levees take their toll on its wetlands.
US states by general coastline (NOAA).Hawaii: The only state made entirely of islands, Hawaii sits roughly 2,400 miles from the nearest continent.
US states by general coastline (NOAA).California: Coast redwoods, the tallest trees on Earth, grow mostly along the foggy northern California coast, while Big Sur's cliffs draw drivers on Highway 1.
US states by general coastline (NOAA).Florida: This state has the longest coastline in the contiguous US, and nowhere in it is more than about 60 miles from salt water.
US states by general coastline (NOAA).Alaska: Alaska's coast makes up over half of the entire US general coastline, and its tidal shoreline is far longer still.

Novels, by word count.The Old Man and the Sea: Hemingway's short novel won the Pulitzer Prize in 1953 and helped him win the Nobel Prize in Literature the next year.
Novels, by word count.The Great Gatsby: Fitzgerald's Jazz Age classic sold poorly at first, and the author died believing it a failure, before becoming a staple of schools.
Novels, by word count.Harry Potter (book 1): The first book about the boy wizard was rejected by around a dozen publishers before Bloomsbury accepted it for a small advance.
Novels, by word count.The Hobbit: Tolkien began this tale as a bedtime story for his children, and it became the prelude to The Lord of the Rings.
Novels, by word count.Pride and Prejudice: Jane Austen's first draft was titled First Impressions, and the book opens with one of the most famous first lines in English.
Novels, by word count.Moby-Dick: Melville's whale epic sold poorly in his lifetime, and it was only rediscovered and praised decades after his death.
Novels, by word count.Ulysses: Joyce's novel follows a single day in Dublin, 16 June 1904, now celebrated every year by fans as Bloomsday.
Novels, by word count.Anna Karenina: Tolstoy's tragic heroine is one of fiction's best-known, and the book's famous first line says that unhappy families are each unhappy in their own way.
Novels, by word count.War and Peace: Tolstoy's epic of Napoleon's invasion of Russia has a vast cast of hundreds of characters, and is often the byword for a really long book.
Novels, by word count.Atlas Shrugged: Ayn Rand's philosophical epic imagines the world's creators going on strike, and it has remained a bestseller for decades.

Powering the world: energy inventions.Volta's battery: Alessandro Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with brine-soaked cardboard, and the volt is named after him.
Powering the world: energy inventions.Faraday's electric motor: This early demonstration made a wire spin around a magnet in a pool of mercury, the first electromagnetic rotation.
Powering the world: energy inventions.Faraday's dynamo: By spinning a copper disc between magnet poles, Faraday made steady electric current, the idea behind generators.
Powering the world: energy inventions.Grove's fuel cell: A Welsh lawyer and scientist combined hydrogen and oxygen to make electricity and water, long before NASA used fuel cells.
Powering the world: energy inventions.Lead-acid battery: Gaston Planté's invention was the first rechargeable battery, and its descendants still start most cars.
Powering the world: energy inventions.Hydroelectric power plant: The Vulcan Street plant in Appleton, Wisconsin, was among the first, and it lit a paper mill and a couple of other buildings.
Powering the world: energy inventions.Electricity-making windmill: Scottish professor James Blyth lit his cottage with one, and Charles Brush built a bigger one in Ohio the next year.
Powering the world: energy inventions.First nuclear reactor: Enrico Fermi's team built it under a Chicago stadium's stands, and it produced a controlled chain reaction.
Powering the world: energy inventions.Silicon solar cell: Bell Labs made the first practical one, about 6 percent efficient, and it soon powered satellites.
Powering the world: energy inventions.Lithium-ion battery on sale: Sony put it on sale, and its inventors shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

How fast humans have moved.Average walking pace: The average walking pace is about 5 km/h, and a healthy human can maintain it for hours, a trait that helped our ancestors travel far.
How fast humans have moved.Elite swimmer (50 m): Even the best swimmers are slow compared with runners, since water is about 800 times denser than air and drags on the body.
How fast humans have moved.Marathon record pace: Marathon records have fallen under two hours and one minute for the world record, which demands holding a sprint-like pace for 42 km.
How fast humans have moved.Usain Bolt at top speed: Usain Bolt hit about 44.7 km/h during his 100 m world record in 2009, and he set it at 9.58 seconds.
How fast humans have moved.Fastest pedal-powered vehicle: Pedal-powered vehicles reach huge speeds when they are streamlined and sit riders in capsules, and some top 140 km/h.
How fast humans have moved.Speed skiing record: Speed skiers wear aerodynamic suits and tuck low down very steep slopes, and the record is above 250 km/h.
How fast humans have moved.Paced bicycle record: Cyclists behind a motorized pace vehicle can go much faster, since the vehicle blocks wind and creates a slipstream.
How fast humans have moved.Baumgartner's freefall: Felix Baumgartner jumped from a balloon at about 39 km up in 2012, and he was the first person to break the speed of sound in freefall.
How fast humans have moved.X-15 rocket plane pilot: The X-15 rocket plane flew to the edge of space in the 1960s, and its pilots reached about Mach 6.
How fast humans have moved.Apollo 10 crew: The Apollo 10 crew holds the human speed record, reached coming back from the Moon in May 1969, and it hasn't been beaten.

Distance from Moscow.St Petersburg: St Petersburg was founded by Peter the Great in 1703, and it was Russia's capital for two centuries, until the Bolsheviks moved it to Moscow.
Distance from Moscow.Kyiv: Kyiv is among the oldest cities in Eastern Europe, and it was the center of Kievan Rus, a medieval state.
Distance from Moscow.Warsaw: Warsaw was largely rebuilt after 1945, and its Old Town was reconstructed from paintings and old photos.
Distance from Moscow.Berlin: Berlin was divided by a wall for 28 years, and the Brandenburg Gate has been a symbol of German reunification.
Distance from Moscow.Rome: Rome is called the Eternal City, and it contains an entire country, Vatican City, within its borders.
Distance from Moscow.Madrid: Madrid is one of Europe's highest capitals, at around 650 m above sea level, and it is home to the famous Prado museum.
Distance from Moscow.New Delhi: New Delhi was designed by British architects in the early twentieth century, and it became India's capital in 1931.
Distance from Moscow.Beijing: Beijing's Forbidden City held 24 emperors across the Ming and Qing dynasties, and it has nearly 1,000 buildings.
Distance from Moscow.New York: New York was once called New Amsterdam, and the Dutch bought, or so the story goes, Manhattan for trinkets worth 60 guilders.
Distance from Moscow.Sydney: Sydney's Opera House took 14 years to build, and its sail-like roof is covered in over a million tiles.

Moonwalkers in the order they stepped ou.Neil Armstrong: Neil Armstrong was first to step onto the Moon in 1969, and he was also the commander who landed with less than a minute of fuel.
Moonwalkers in the order they stepped ou.Buzz Aldrin: Buzz Aldrin followed Armstrong, and he also took the first selfie in space, and walked on the Moon about 20 minutes later.
Moonwalkers in the order they stepped ou.Pete Conrad: Pete Conrad was the third man to walk on the Moon, and he joked about his height after Armstrong's one small step quote.
Moonwalkers in the order they stepped ou.Alan Bean: Alan Bean became a painter after his Apollo 12 mission, and he used lunar dust in his paintings.
Moonwalkers in the order they stepped ou.Alan Shepard: Alan Shepard hit golf balls on the Moon using a makeshift club, and he had been the first American in space.
Moonwalkers in the order they stepped ou.Edgar Mitchell: Edgar Mitchell conducted ESP experiments during his flight, and later founded the Institute of Noetic Sciences.
Moonwalkers in the order they stepped ou.David Scott: David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, showing that they fall at the same rate without air.
Moonwalkers in the order they stepped ou.John Young: John Young later commanded the first space shuttle flight, and he is the only person to fly in Gemini, Apollo and shuttle missions.
Moonwalkers in the order they stepped ou.Charlie Duke: Charlie Duke left a family photo on the Moon, and it is still sitting in the lunar dust.
Moonwalkers in the order they stepped ou.Harrison Schmitt: Harrison Schmitt was the only professional geologist to walk on the Moon, and he was the next-to-last man to leave it.

US Navy officer ranks.Ensign: The entry-level officer rank; the word comes from ensign meaning flag bearer, as the junior officer once carried the colors.
US Navy officer ranks.Lieutenant (junior grade): Usually shortened to LTJG, it sits between ensign and lieutenant, and officers are usually promoted to it after about two years.
US Navy officer ranks.Lieutenant: A naval lieutenant outranks an army lieutenant; its pay grade matches an army captain, which confuses newcomers.
US Navy officer ranks.Lieutenant Commander: Equal in pay grade to an army major, it is a common rank for department heads and executive officers on warships.
US Navy officer ranks.Commander: Often given charge of a ship or squadron; the equivalent army rank is lieutenant colonel.
US Navy officer ranks.Captain: This rank matches an army colonel, though whoever commands any ship is called captain regardless of rank.
US Navy officer ranks.Rear Admiral (lower half): A one-star rank that replaced the old commodore rank in 1985; the 'lower half' refers to its seniority within the grade.
US Navy officer ranks.Rear Admiral: The first rank with two stars, rear admirals often command task forces or oversee entire fleets of ships.
US Navy officer ranks.Vice Admiral: Three-star officers typically lead major fleets or serve in top posts at headquarters.
US Navy officer ranks.Admiral: This four-star rank is the top peacetime Navy rank; five-star fleet admiral has not been used since World War II.

Eurovision winners by year.ABBA, Waterloo: ABBA won with 'Waterloo' and the performance launched their global career, and it is regarded by many as the best Eurovision winner ever.
Eurovision winners by year.Bucks Fizz: Bucks Fizz won with 'Making Your Mind Up', and the skirt-ripping dance move that was part of the act has become legendary.
Eurovision winners by year.Céline Dion (for Switzerland): Céline Dion won for Switzerland with 'Ne partez pas sans moi' by a single point, and her global stardom followed.
Eurovision winners by year.Katrina and the Waves: Katrina and the Waves won for the UK with 'Love Shine a Light', the last UK win to date.
Eurovision winners by year.Dana International: Dana International, an Israeli singer, became the first openly transgender winner of the contest, with 'Diva'.
Eurovision winners by year.Lordi: Lordi, a Finnish hard-rock band in monster costumes, won with 'Hard Rock Hallelujah', giving Finland its first win.
Eurovision winners by year.Loreen, Euphoria: Loreen won for Sweden with 'Euphoria', which topped the charts across Europe, and she won again in 2023.
Eurovision winners by year.Conchita Wurst: Conchita Wurst, the bearded drag persona of Austrian singer Tom Neuwirth, won with 'Rise Like a Phoenix'.
Eurovision winners by year.Netta, Toy: Netta won for Israel with 'Toy', a song which included clucking chicken noises and loop-pedal beats.
Eurovision winners by year.Måneskin: Måneskin, an Italian rock band, won in Rotterdam with 'Zitti e buoni', and later became international stars.

When these organizations were founded.The Jesuits: Ignatius of Loyola founded the Society of Jesus; its schools spread worldwide, and Pope Francis was the first Jesuit pope.
When these organizations were founded.Dutch East India Company: The VOC is widely regarded as the first publicly traded company, selling shares in Amsterdam.
When these organizations were founded.Hudson's Bay Company: Chartered by Charles II, its fur trade shaped Canada's map, and its grant covered the huge Rupert's Land watershed.
When these organizations were founded.Red Cross: Henri Dunant founded it after seeing the carnage at Solferino, and its emblem reverses the Swiss flag.
When these organizations were founded.Intl. Olympic Committee: Pierre de Coubertin founded it at the Sorbonne in Paris, and the first modern Games were held in Athens in 1896.
When these organizations were founded.League of Nations: It was created after the First World War by the Versailles settlement, but the US never joined, and the UN replaced it.
When these organizations were founded.United Nations: Its charter was signed in San Francisco in June 1945 and entered into force that October with 51 founding members.
When these organizations were founded.NATO: Its Article 5 says an attack on one member is an attack on all, invoked only once, after the September 11 attacks.
When these organizations were founded.OPEC: Five countries founded it in Baghdad: Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.
When these organizations were founded.European Union: The Maastricht Treaty took effect in November 1993, and the euro followed as a currency in 1999.

When these iconic photos were taken.Lunch atop a Skyscraper: Staged for publicity during construction of Rockefeller Center, it shows ironworkers eating on a girder high above Manhattan.
When these iconic photos were taken.Migrant Mother: Dorothea Lange's portrait of Florence Owens Thompson, a pea picker, became the defining image of the Great Depression.
When these iconic photos were taken.Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima: Joe Rosenthal's picture won a Pulitzer within months. It actually shows the second flag raising that day, with a larger replacement flag.
When these iconic photos were taken.Che's 'Guerrillero Heroico': Alberto Korda took it at a memorial service and never charged for it. It became one of the most reproduced images in history.
When these iconic photos were taken.Earthrise: Astronaut Bill Anders took it while orbiting the Moon on Apollo 8, and it is often credited with inspiring the environmental movement.
When these iconic photos were taken.'Napalm Girl': Nick Ut's photo of nine-year-old Kim Phuc fleeing a napalm strike. She survived, later moved to Canada and became a UNESCO goodwill ambassador.
When these iconic photos were taken.Afghan Girl: Steve McCurry's portrait for National Geographic. Its subject, Sharbat Gula, was found and identified in 2002 by her striking eyes.
When these iconic photos were taken.Tank Man: A lone man stood in front of a column of tanks near Tiananmen Square the day after the crackdown. His identity is still unknown.
When these iconic photos were taken.The Falling Man: Richard Drew's photo of a man falling from the World Trade Center ran in papers once, then sparked a long debate over showing such images.
When these iconic photos were taken.The Situation Room: Pete Souza's photo shows Obama and his team watching the raid on Osama bin Laden; Hillary Clinton's covered mouth became its signature detail.

Refractive index: how much they bend lig.Vacuum: By definition it is exactly 1, and nothing in the universe travels faster than light in a vacuum.
Refractive index: how much they bend lig.Air: Tiny changes in the index of air, from heat or altitude, cause mirages and make stars twinkle.
Refractive index: how much they bend lig.Ice: Snow looks white because its ice crystals scatter light in all directions, even though clear ice is transparent.
Refractive index: how much they bend lig.Water: Light slows to about 75 percent of its vacuum speed in water, which is why a straw looks bent in a glass.
Refractive index: how much they bend lig.Crown glass: Opticians pair it with flint glass to cancel color fringes in lenses, a combination invented in the 1700s.
Refractive index: how much they bend lig.Sapphire: It is the same mineral as ruby, corundum, and is used for scratch-resistant watch crystals, since it is very hard.
Refractive index: how much they bend lig.Cubic zirconia: This diamond simulant actually flashes more rainbow colors than the real thing, because of its high dispersion.
Refractive index: how much they bend lig.Diamond: Its high index and dispersion create the sparkle, with light trapped inside by total internal reflection.
Refractive index: how much they bend lig.Moissanite: Henri Moissan first found it in a meteorite crater in Arizona in 1893, and most of it today is lab-grown.
Refractive index: how much they bend lig.Germanium (infrared): Opaque to our eyes but transparent to infrared, it is used for thermal camera lenses and night-vision optics.

Great psychologists, by birth year.Wilhelm Wundt: Founded the first psychology laboratory, at Leipzig in 1879, a date often used for when psychology became a science apart from philosophy.
Great psychologists, by birth year.William James: Brother of novelist Henry James, he wrote The Principles of Psychology and described consciousness as a continuous 'stream'.
Great psychologists, by birth year.Ivan Pavlov: His 1904 Nobel Prize was for research on digestion, and it was while studying digestive reflexes that he noticed the dogs' conditioned salivation.
Great psychologists, by birth year.Alfred Adler: He coined the term 'inferiority complex' and broke with Freud to found his own school, individual psychology.
Great psychologists, by birth year.Carl Jung: Introduced introversion and extraversion, and the idea of archetypes shared by all humans in what he called the collective unconscious.
Great psychologists, by birth year.Jean Piaget: He began by studying children's wrong answers on intelligence tests, which led him to his stages of cognitive development.
Great psychologists, by birth year.B. F. Skinner: He built the operant conditioning chamber, nicknamed the Skinner box, and also devised a climate-controlled 'air crib' for his daughter.
Great psychologists, by birth year.Abraham Maslow: His hierarchy of needs is usually drawn as a pyramid, though Maslow himself never drew it that way.
Great psychologists, by birth year.Stanley Milgram: His 1961 obedience experiments found about 65 percent of volunteers delivered what they believed was the maximum shock; he also ran the small-world study.
Great psychologists, by birth year.Steven Pinker: A Harvard cognitive scientist who wrote The Language Instinct, arguing that language is an evolved ability of the human mind.

How much data these game media hold.Atari 2600 Combat cartridge: Combat's 2 KB is smaller than a short email, yet it came packed with tank and plane duels for two players.
How much data these game media hold.Game Boy Tetris cartridge: Tetris fit in 32 KB, about the size of a small image today, and shipped with the Game Boy, making that handheld a must-have.
How much data these game media hold.NES Super Mario Bros. cart: About 40 KB, smaller than many web images, yet it fit eight worlds of running, jumping and mushrooms.
How much data these game media hold.3.5-inch floppy disk: The 3.5-inch disk held 1.44 MB, and its hard plastic shell made it sturdier than the floppy disks that came before.
How much data these game media hold.Super Mario 64 cartridge: Its 8 MB cartridge held a fully 3D world, but was costly to make, which pushed Nintendo's rivals toward cheaper CDs.
How much data these game media hold.CD-ROM: A CD-ROM held about 650 MB, which was enough for hours of music or full-motion video, and it ended the cartridge era for many PC games.
How much data these game media hold.GameCube mini disc: Nintendo's GameCube used small 8-centimetre discs, which could not be read by standard DVD players.
How much data these game media hold.DVD (single layer): A single-layer DVD held 4.7 GB, and the PlayStation 2 used it to play games and movies, and was a cheap DVD player for many families.
How much data these game media hold.Blu-ray (single layer): A single-layer Blu-ray holds 25 GB; it beat HD DVD in the format war partly because the PlayStation 3 had a Blu-ray drive.
How much data these game media hold.Blu-ray (dual layer): A dual-layer Blu-ray holds 50 GB, enough for a big game, and the format was named for the blue-violet laser that reads it.

When these everyday inventions first app.Friction match: English chemist John Walker sold the first ones in Stockton-on-Tees, and he never patented his invention.
When these everyday inventions first app.Postage stamp: The Penny Black carried a profile of Queen Victoria and was the world's first adhesive postage stamp.
When these everyday inventions first app.Barbed wire: Joseph Glidden's patent helped fence the American West and changed ranching forever.
When these everyday inventions first app.Telephone: Bell filed his patent the same day Elisha Gray filed a caveat, a famous race.
When these everyday inventions first app.Band-Aid: Earle Dickson invented it at Johnson & Johnson for his wife, who kept cutting her fingers.
When these everyday inventions first app.Sliced bread: Otto Rohwedder's machine produced the first loaves in Chillicothe, Missouri.
When these everyday inventions first app.Ballpoint pen (Biro): Hungarian László Bíró designed it, and the RAF used it, since fountain pens leaked at altitude.
When these everyday inventions first app.Microwave oven: Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket near a radar magnetron.
When these everyday inventions first app.Diners Club charge card: The story goes that it was invented after a man forgot his wallet at a restaurant.
When these everyday inventions first app.Bubble wrap: It was originally invented as textured wallpaper before becoming packaging.

Chinese characters, by number of strokes.人 (person): The character resembles a person walking on two legs, and it is one of the simplest and most common characters.
Chinese characters, by number of strokes.口 (mouth): This simple square is the building block of many characters about speaking or eating, and it also means mouth.
Chinese characters, by number of strokes.木 (tree): Add a second and you get 林 (forest); add a third and you get 森 (a thick forest).
Chinese characters, by number of strokes.生 (life): It can mean life, birth, or raw, and is one of the most versatile characters in the language.
Chinese characters, by number of strokes.字 (character): It combines a roof and a child, and originally meant to nurture, before coming to mean a written character.
Chinese characters, by number of strokes.言 (speech): It is the radical in many words about speaking, and it also appears in characters such as 語 and 話.
Chinese characters, by number of strokes.金 (gold): It is the radical for metals, and stands for gold itself; it also appears in the Chinese word for money.
Chinese characters, by number of strokes.星 (star): It places the sun 日 over 生, and it has nine strokes, as a picture of bright points of light.
Chinese characters, by number of strokes.書 (book): The traditional form has 10 strokes, while the simplified 书 has only four.
Chinese characters, by number of strokes.龍 (dragon): The traditional form takes 16 strokes, while the simplified 龙 takes just five, and the mythical beast symbolizes luck.

Disney live-action remakes by release.101 Dalmatians (live-action): Glenn Close played Cruella, and the film sparked a surge in Dalmatian purchases.
Disney live-action remakes by release.Alice in Wonderland: Tim Burton's film grossed over a billion dollars and set off Disney's remake wave.
Disney live-action remakes by release.Maleficent: It retells Sleeping Beauty from the villain's point of view, starring Angelina Jolie.
Disney live-action remakes by release.Cinderella: Directed by Kenneth Branagh, it stayed closer to the 1950 animated film than later remakes did.
Disney live-action remakes by release.The Jungle Book: Nearly all of it, jungle included, was made in a Los Angeles studio with newcomer Neel Sethi the only live actor.
Disney live-action remakes by release.Beauty and the Beast: It grossed over $1.2 billion and starred Emma Watson.
Disney live-action remakes by release.The Lion King: It was made with photoreal computer animation, no live action, yet grossed over $1.6 billion.
Disney live-action remakes by release.Mulan: It skipped theaters in many markets for Disney+ Premier Access; the story comes from the Ballad of Mulan.
Disney live-action remakes by release.The Little Mermaid: Halle Bailey starred, and Alan Menken's songs from the 1989 original returned.
Disney live-action remakes by release.Snow White: It remakes the 1937 film that was Disney's first animated feature.

How much these hold.Teaspoon: Cutlery teaspoons vary, so recipes use a standard measure fixed at five millilitres.
How much these hold.Tablespoon: In Australia a tablespoon is 20 ml, not 15, so imported recipes can come out different.
How much these hold.Single espresso: A shot is made by forcing hot water through about seven grams of finely ground coffee at high pressure.
How much these hold.US soda can: A regular can of cola contains around 39 grams of sugar, about ten teaspoons.
How much these hold.Wine bottle: One theory for 750 ml is that a standard 225-litre barrel fills exactly 300 bottles.
How much these hold.Full electric kettle: The electric kettle was invented in the 1890s, in an effort to boil water without a stove.
How much these hold.US gallon of milk: The American gallon is smaller than the imperial one used in Britain, which holds about 4.55 litres.
How much these hold.Car fuel tank: A full tank holds about 450 kilowatt-hours of chemical energy, several times a typical electric car's battery.
How much these hold.Filled bathtub: Archimedes's bath, according to legend, led him to the principle of displacement, so rising water means an object takes up space.
How much these hold.Olympic swimming pool: The two-metre minimum depth is deliberate, since deeper water calms waves and makes for faster races.

Major key signatures, flats to sharps.E♭ major: Beethoven's heroic key, used for his Eroica Symphony, whose title means heroic.
Major key signatures, flats to sharps.B♭ major: The natural key for clarinets and trumpets, which are pitched in B♭.
Major key signatures, flats to sharps.F major: Beethoven's Pastoral Symphony is in this key, which has a single flat, B♭.
Major key signatures, flats to sharps.C major: Its scale uses only the white piano keys, and Mozart's much-loved easy sonata K. 545 is in it.
Major key signatures, flats to sharps.G major: Open violin strings make it ring beautifully, and its one sharp is F♯.
Major key signatures, flats to sharps.D major: Violinists love its brilliance, and Pachelbel's Canon is in it.
Major key signatures, flats to sharps.A major: Mozart's Clarinet Concerto is in this key, which has three sharps.
Major key signatures, flats to sharps.E major: Guitarists love it because the low open E string rings along with its chords.
Major key signatures, flats to sharps.B major: It is enharmonic with C♭ major, which would need seven flats instead of five sharps.
Major key signatures, flats to sharps.F♯ major: Its six sharps are the same notes as G♭ major's six flats, a rare tie where both spellings are used.

Numbers by how many divisors they have.8: Its divisors are 1, 2, 4 and 8, because it is a prime cubed.
Numbers by how many divisors they have.12: A dozen divides neatly by 2, 3, 4 and 6, one reason we count eggs and hours in twelves.
Numbers by how many divisors they have.13: A prime number: its only divisors are 1 and itself, the fewest any number above 1 can have.
Numbers by how many divisors they have.16: A power of two, with divisors 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. Every power of two has one more divisor than its exponent.
Numbers by how many divisors they have.24: Its eight divisors help explain why a day is split into 24 hours.
Numbers by how many divisors they have.25: The square of a prime. Any such number has exactly three divisors: 1, 5 and 25.
Numbers by how many divisors they have.36: Perfect squares always have an odd number of divisors, and 36 has nine.
Numbers by how many divisors they have.60: The Babylonians counted in sixties because it divides so evenly, which is why we have 60 minutes and seconds.
Numbers by how many divisors they have.64: Seven divisors, as 2 to the sixth power. It is also the number of squares on a chessboard.
Numbers by how many divisors they have.360: Its many divisors are often cited as the reason a circle is cut into 360 degrees.

Inventions behind modern electronics.Transistor: Invented at Bell Labs by Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley, who won the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Inventions behind modern electronics.Integrated circuit: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce at Fairchild developed it independently. Kilby won a Nobel Prize in 2000.
Inventions behind modern electronics.Laser: Theodore Maiman built the first working one using a ruby crystal.
Inventions behind modern electronics.Computer mouse demo: Douglas Engelbart showed it at the famous 1968 'Mother of All Demos'. His first mouse had a wooden shell.
Inventions behind modern electronics.Floppy disk: IBM's first ones were 8 inches wide and held only a few hundred kilobytes.
Inventions behind modern electronics.Ethernet: Robert Metcalfe devised it at Xerox PARC, and its name nods to the old idea of a light-carrying 'ether'.
Inventions behind modern electronics.Compact Disc: Philips and Sony's disc, first sold in Japan in 1982, changed how music was sold.
Inventions behind modern electronics.QR code: Masahiro Hara of Denso Wave invented it to track car parts, and its name stands for Quick Response.
Inventions behind modern electronics.GPS fully operational: Run by the US military, the system was declared fully operational in 1995. Civilian signals were sharpened in 2000.
Inventions behind modern electronics.Bluetooth 1.0: Named after Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century Danish king who united tribes. The logo combines his initials as runes.

Continents and oceans by area.Australia: The smallest continent is also a single country, and it's the only one that is both a nation and a continent.
Continents and oceans by area.Europe: Europe is technically a western peninsula of Eurasia, and its border with Asia is a cultural convention along the Urals.
Continents and oceans by area.Arctic Ocean: The smallest and shallowest ocean is mostly covered by sea ice, and it's warming faster than anywhere else.
Continents and oceans by area.South America: It holds the Amazon, the world's biggest river by volume, and the Andes, the longest mountain range above water.
Continents and oceans by area.North America: It contains the Great Lakes, the largest group of freshwater lakes on Earth, and runs from the Arctic to Panama.
Continents and oceans by area.Africa: The second-largest continent, it has the Sahara and the Nile, and it's the only one that crosses both the equator and both tropics.
Continents and oceans by area.Asia: The biggest continent holds roughly 60 percent of the world's people, plus Everest and the Dead Sea's low point.
Continents and oceans by area.Indian Ocean: It's the only ocean named for a country, and its monsoon winds guided sailors' trade routes for millennia.
Continents and oceans by area.Atlantic Ocean: It's named for the Titan Atlas, and it separates the Old World from the New, growing slightly wider each year.
Continents and oceans by area.Pacific Ocean: The Pacific covers about a third of the Earth's surface, more than all land together, and holds the Mariana Trench.

How long these medieval figures lived.Emperor Otto III: The teenage emperor died at 21, and had dreamed of restoring Rome, with Gerbert of Aurillac, later pope, as his tutor.
How long these medieval figures lived.Henry V of England: The hero of Agincourt in Shakespeare died of illness at 35, probably dysentery, and left a nine-month-old son as king.
How long these medieval figures lived.Richard the Lionheart: He died of a crossbow wound from an arrow at Châlus, and the English king's heart is buried in Rouen.
How long these medieval figures lived.Edward the Black Prince: Edward the Black Prince beat the French at Poitiers and captured their king, but died a year before his father, never becoming king.
How long these medieval figures lived.Thomas Aquinas: The Italian theologian wrote the Summa Theologica, and died on his way to a church council; he was nicknamed the 'Dumb Ox'.
How long these medieval figures lived.Dante Alighieri: The Florentine poet wrote the Divine Comedy in exile, and died in Ravenna at 56.
How long these medieval figures lived.Ibn Battuta: The Moroccan traveler journeyed some 120,000 km across the Islamic world and beyond, and he dictated his book from memory.
How long these medieval figures lived.Kublai Khan: Genghis Khan's grandson ruled China as the first Yuan emperor, and hosted Marco Polo, according to Polo's accounts.
How long these medieval figures lived.Eleanor of Aquitaine: She was queen of France and then England, and went on a Crusade, and outlived most of her ten children.
How long these medieval figures lived.Doge Enrico Dandolo: The blind Venetian doge led the Fourth Crusade to sack Constantinople at about 90, and the city's famous bronze horses came to Venice from it.

The Labors of Heracles, in order.Nemean Lion: The beast's hide was proof against any weapon, so Heracles strangled it and wore its pelt as armour.
The Labors of Heracles, in order.Lernaean Hydra: Each time a head was cut off, two grew back, until Heracles' nephew Iolaus seared the stumps with fire.
The Labors of Heracles, in order.Erymanthian Boar: Heracles chased it into deep snow, and when he brought it back alive the king hid in a bronze jar.
The Labors of Heracles, in order.Augean Stables: He cleaned the stables in a day by diverting two rivers through them, and 'Augean' now means filthy.
The Labors of Heracles, in order.Stymphalian Birds: The man-eating birds had bronze beaks, and Heracles scared them from hiding with a rattle given by Athena.
The Labors of Heracles, in order.Cretan Bull: Poseidon's bull was linked in myth to the birth of the Minotaur, and Heracles brought it back to Greece.
The Labors of Heracles, in order.Mares of Diomedes: Heracles fed their cruel owner, King Diomedes, to his own horses, which were said to eat human flesh.
The Labors of Heracles, in order.Belt of Hippolyta: The Amazon queen's belt was a gift from the war god Ares, and the labor reportedly ended in a battle with the Amazons.
The Labors of Heracles, in order.Apples of the Hesperides: Atlas fetched them while Heracles held up the sky for him, and the golden apples were guarded by a hundred-headed dragon.
The Labors of Heracles, in order.Cerberus: Only this labor took Heracles to the underworld, where he had to bring back the three-headed hound of Hades.

Their birthdays, through the calendar ye.Elvis Presley: Born in a two-room house in Tupelo, Mississippi, he had a twin brother who died at birth.
Born Michael King Jr., his father changed both their names after a trip to Germany; his birthday is a US holiday on the third Monday of January.
Their birthdays, through the calendar ye.Abraham Lincoln: He shares the day, in 1809, with Charles Darwin.
Their birthdays, through the calendar ye.Albert Einstein: He was born in Ulm, Germany, and his birthday falls on Pi Day.
Their birthdays, through the calendar ye.William Shakespeare: The date is traditional, because only his baptism on 26 April is recorded, and he is also said to have died on the same date.
Their birthdays, through the calendar ye.Marilyn Monroe: She was born Norma Jeane Mortenson, and the birthday falls in the middle of the year.
Their birthdays, through the calendar ye.Princess Diana: Born at Park House, on the Sandringham estate, she was known as Lady Diana Spencer until her marriage.
Their birthdays, through the calendar ye.Napoleon Bonaparte: He was born in Corsica a year after the island passed from Genoa to France.
Their birthdays, through the calendar ye.Mahatma Gandhi: The date is now marked as the International Day of Non-Violence.
Their birthdays, through the calendar ye.Isaac Newton: The date is Old Style, as Britain used the Julian calendar, and by the modern one it was 4 January 1643.

Monopoly (US) property prices.Baltic Avenue: Baltic shares the cheapest price on the board with Mediterranean. Like the other streets, it is named after a real Atlantic City street.
Monopoly (US) property prices.Oriental Avenue: Oriental is one of the light-blue trio. Monopoly's roots go back to Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to show the evils of landlords.
Monopoly (US) property prices.Connecticut Avenue: Connecticut is the light-blue set's priciest street, and the third property you need to own to start building houses there.
Monopoly (US) property prices.Virginia Avenue: Part of the pink set, it carries Atlantic City's real street names; Charles Darrow sold his version of the game to Parker Brothers in 1935.
Monopoly (US) property prices.New York Avenue: Orange properties like this are among the most profitable, because a trip to Jail tends to leave players a few rolls away from them.
Monopoly (US) property prices.Illinois Avenue: Illinois Avenue is statistically among the most landed-on squares, because Chance cards and the Jail routes send players that way.
Monopoly (US) property prices.Marvin Gardens: The real Atlantic City district is 'Marven Gardens'. Monopoly's makers misspelled it, and the typo stuck.
Monopoly (US) property prices.Pennsylvania Avenue: The green set's costliest-to-build street can charge well over a thousand dollars in rent once it has a hotel.
Monopoly (US) property prices.Park Place: Park Place is one half of the dark-blue duo, named after a real Atlantic City street, though the actual street is far more modest.
Monopoly (US) property prices.Boardwalk: Atlantic City's Boardwalk, built in 1870, is often called America's first. The game made its name a byword for the top of the board.

The Christmas story, in order.Gabriel visits Mary: The archangel's visit is the Annunciation, celebrated on March 25, exactly nine months before Christmas.
The Christmas story, in order.Mary visits Elizabeth: Luke says the baby John the Baptist leaps in Elizabeth's womb when Mary arrives.
The Christmas story, in order.Journey to Bethlehem: The couple travel from Nazareth for a Roman census, a trip of many days on foot or donkey.
The Christmas story, in order.Born in a manger: A manger is a feeding trough for animals, and Luke's no room at the inn may mean a guest room.
The Christmas story, in order.Angels appear to shepherds: Only Luke's gospel has the shepherds, and the angels' song became Glory to God in the highest.
The Christmas story, in order.Shepherds visit the baby: Shepherds were humble working people, the first to hear the news in Luke's telling.
The Christmas story, in order.Wise men meet Herod: Matthew's Magi ask where to find the newborn King of the Jews, alarming Herod.
The Christmas story, in order.Wise men bring gifts: Matthew names gold, frankincense and myrrh but never says three men or that they were kings; those traditions grew later.
The Christmas story, in order.Flight into Egypt: Warned in a dream, Joseph takes the family to Egypt to escape Herod; it is a favorite subject in art.
The Christmas story, in order.Massacre of the Innocents: Only Matthew recounts Herod ordering the deaths of Bethlehem's boys; it is remembered on December 28 as Holy Innocents' Day.

Bible books, by number of chapters.Revelation: The last book of the New Testament, whose Greek name 'Apocalypse' means 'unveiling', was written on the island of Patmos.
Bible books, by number of chapters.Matthew: Placed first in the New Testament, it holds the Sermon on the Mount, including the Beatitudes.
Bible books, by number of chapters.Numbers: The title refers to two censuses of Israel; the Hebrew name Bamidbar means 'in the wilderness'.
Bible books, by number of chapters.Exodus: Greek for 'departure', it tells of the escape from Egypt and the giving of the Ten Commandments.
Bible books, by number of chapters.Job: A poetic book about suffering, it gave us the phrase 'the patience of Job'.
Bible books, by number of chapters.Ezekiel: It contains the vision of the valley of dry bones, which came to life.
Bible books, by number of chapters.Genesis: Its Hebrew title, 'Bereshit', is just the first word, meaning 'in the beginning'.
Bible books, by number of chapters.Jeremiah: By word count, it is the longest book in the Hebrew Bible, and its prophet was nicknamed the 'weeping prophet'.
Bible books, by number of chapters.Isaiah: A complete Isaiah scroll found among the Dead Sea Scrolls is about seven metres long.
Bible books, by number of chapters.Psalms: It holds Psalm 119, the longest chapter in the Bible, and Psalm 117, the shortest.

Weigh-in: from mouse to monument.A house mouse: A house mouse's heart beats several hundred times a minute. Despite the weight, it can fit through a gap about the width of a pencil.
Weigh-in: from mouse to monument.A baseball: A baseball's red stitches number 108 and are done by hand. The ball weighs between about 142 and 149 grams.
Weigh-in: from mouse to monument.A basketball: The standard men's ball must bounce back to a set height when dropped from about 1.8 metres. Its pebbled surface helps grip.
Weigh-in: from mouse to monument.A bowling ball (max): The maximum weight in tenpin bowling is 16 pounds. It's a famously heavy thing to hold in one hand, with thumb and finger holes.
Weigh-in: from mouse to monument.A golden retriever: Golden retrievers were bred in 19th-century Scotland to retrieve shot waterfowl without damaging it. Their soft mouths are why.
Weigh-in: from mouse to monument.A concert grand piano: A concert grand has up to 230 strings under a combined tension of around 20 tonnes. That tension is held by a cast-iron frame.
Weigh-in: from mouse to monument.A family car: The average family car weighs about 1,500 kg, roughly 250 times a baseball. Modern electric cars are often heavier thanks to their batteries.
Weigh-in: from mouse to monument.An African elephant: The African elephant is the largest land animal, and an adult male can be four metres at the shoulder. It eats up to about 150 kg of plants a day.
Weigh-in: from mouse to monument.A Boeing 747 (empty): An empty 747 has a wingspan of about 60 metres. Fully loaded it can weigh over 350 tonnes at takeoff.
Weigh-in: from mouse to monument.The Eiffel Tower: The tower is about 7,300 tonnes of wrought iron structure, and it grows around 15 cm taller on hot days. It's repainted about every seven years.

Basketball by the numbers.Players on court per team: James Naismith's original 1891 game used nine players a side, then five became standard. Teams of five still pass and cut in sync.
Basketball by the numbers.Fouls to foul out (NBA): Six personal fouls and a player is out in the NBA, while international rules set it at five. Stars in foul trouble often sit on the bench.
Basketball by the numbers.Rim height (ft): The hoop stays at 10 feet at every level, since Naismith's original peach baskets hung from a gym balcony that high. It has never changed.
Basketball by the numbers.Free-throw distance (ft): The free-throw line is 15 feet from the backboard's plane. Each successful shot is worth one point, and the shooter is unguarded.
Basketball by the numbers.NBA lane width (ft): The lane was widened from 12 to 16 feet in 1964, partly to limit the dominance of Wilt Chamberlain. It's often called "the paint."
Basketball by the numbers.NBA three at the top (ft): The NBA adopted the three-point line in 1979. It curves out to this distance at the top, but only 22 feet in the corners.
Basketball by the numbers.Ball circumference (in): The ball must measure about 29.5 inches around for men's play, and 28.5 for women's. Its orange colour helps spectators see it.
Basketball by the numbers.NBA court width (ft): An NBA court is 50 feet wide, which is narrower than a tennis court's length. International courts are a bit narrower.
Basketball by the numbers.Backboard width (in): The backboard is six feet wide, and its rectangle on the glass helps shooters aim bank shots. Glass boards replaced wood and wire mesh ones.
Basketball by the numbers.NBA court length (ft): A pro court is 94 feet long, and a fast-break sprint covers it in only a few seconds. Both baskets and benches sit along the same length.

Spin-off TV series premieres.The Jeffersons: Spun off from All in the Family, George and Louise Jefferson were 'moving on up' to a deluxe apartment in the sky.
Spin-off TV series premieres.Laverne & Shirley: Spun off from Happy Days, the L on Laverne's sweater is her initial, and it starred Penny Marshall.
Spin-off TV series premieres.Mork & Mindy: Robin Williams' alien debuted on Happy Days before getting his own show, which launched Williams to stardom.
Spin-off TV series premieres.Frasier: Spun off from Cheers, it ran 11 seasons and won a record 37 Emmys, a record then for a comedy.
Spin-off TV series premieres.Daria: The cynical teen spun off from Beavis and Butt-Head, and became an icon of the 1990s.
Spin-off TV series premieres.Joey: A Friends spin-off that ran two seasons, following Matt LeBlanc's actor in Los Angeles.
Spin-off TV series premieres.Torchwood: A Doctor Who spin-off whose title is an anagram of Doctor Who, centered on a Cardiff team fighting aliens.
Spin-off TV series premieres.Better Call Saul: A prequel to Breaking Bad, which followed Jimmy McGill before he became Saul Goodman.
Spin-off TV series premieres.Young Sheldon: A prequel to The Big Bang Theory that follows the genius as a child in Texas.
Spin-off TV series premieres.House of the Dragon: A prequel to Game of Thrones about the Targaryen civil war, known as the Dance of the Dragons.

How tall these medieval towers are.White Tower, London: Begun around 1078 as the core of the Tower of London, it was once the tallest building in the city.
How tall these medieval towers are.Kalyan Minaret, Bukhara: Built in 1127, Genghis Khan reportedly spared it in 1220, impressed by its height, while razing the rest of the city.
How tall these medieval towers are.Leaning Tower of Pisa: Construction started in 1173 and it began to lean while still going up, because of soft ground.
How tall these medieval towers are.Minaret of Jam: It stands in a remote Afghan gorge, and its brickwork is covered in turquoise calligraphy.
How tall these medieval towers are.Qutub Minar: Begun in 1193 in Delhi, it is often described as the world's tallest brick minaret.
How tall these medieval towers are.Giotto's Campanile: Giotto designed it in 1334 but died three years later, and others finished the work.
How tall these medieval towers are.Asinelli Tower, Bologna: It has about 500 steps up, and it leans slightly, like its neighbor the Garisenda.
How tall these medieval towers are.Torrazzo of Cremona: It is the tallest brick bell tower in Italy, in the city that gave the world Stradivari's violins.
How tall these medieval towers are.Salisbury Cathedral spire: Its 14th-century spire is the tallest in the UK, and its weight has bent the pillars below.
How tall these medieval towers are.Strasbourg Cathedral: It was the tallest building in the world from 1647 until 1874.

Old-fashioned units of length.Thou (mil): A human hair is only about three thou thick, which shows how fine this unit is.
Old-fashioned units of length.Barleycorn: English units were once based on the barleycorn, and shoe sizes still step in barleycorns.
Old-fashioned units of length.Hand: Horses are still measured in these, with a hand being four inches.
Old-fashioned units of length.Span: Roughly the stretch between your thumb and little finger when your hand is spread wide.
Old-fashioned units of length.English ell: A cloth merchant's unit, behind the proverb 'give them an inch and they'll take an ell'.
Old-fashioned units of length.Fathom: Sailors measured water depth in these, and 'mark twain' meant two fathoms.
Old-fashioned units of length.Rod: An acre was traditionally four rods by forty, so this unit is hidden in land measurement.
Old-fashioned units of length.Chain: A cricket pitch is exactly one of these long, from Gunter's surveying chain.
Old-fashioned units of length.Furlong: Short for 'furrow long', the distance a team of oxen plowed; there are eight in a mile.
Old-fashioned units of length.League: Roughly the distance a person could walk in an hour, and Jules Verne's 20,000 of them are about distance traveled, not depth.

Star Wars (1977), scene by scene.Leia hides plans in R2-D2: The 1977 film was later retitled Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope.
Star Wars (1977), scene by scene.Jawas sell the droids: Tatooine's name comes from Tataouine, a real town in Tunisia where scenes were filmed.
Star Wars (1977), scene by scene.Luke sees Leia's message: R2-D2's beeps and whistles were designed by sound designer Ben Burtt.
Star Wars (1977), scene by scene.Obi-Wan saves Luke: Alec Guinness took a small share of the film's profits, which made him wealthy.
Star Wars (1977), scene by scene.Luke's home is burned: Owen and Beru Lars are Luke's aunt and uncle, and their moisture farm is on the desert planet Tatooine.
Star Wars (1977), scene by scene.Hiring Han Solo at the cantina: John Williams wrote the Cantina Band tune, and Han claims the Falcon made the Kessel Run in under twelve parsecs.
Star Wars (1977), scene by scene.Alderaan is destroyed: Alderaan's destruction shows the Death Star's power, and Governor Tarkin orders it.
Star Wars (1977), scene by scene.Rescuing Leia from her cell: Leia's line Aren't you a little short for a stormtrooper? is one of the film's best-loved.
Star Wars (1977), scene by scene.Vader strikes down Obi-Wan: Vader's body was actor David Prowse, and his voice was James Earl Jones.
Star Wars (1977), scene by scene.Luke destroys the Death Star: The Death Star's weakness is a tiny exhaust port that a proton torpedo can reach.

Mahatma Gandhi's life, in order.Born: Gandhi was born in Porbandar, Gujarat, in 1869, to a family of local officials, and his full name was Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi.
Mahatma Gandhi's life, in order.Marries Kasturba: Gandhi was married at 13 in an arranged marriage to Kasturba, who was the same age and later joined his campaigns.
Mahatma Gandhi's life, in order.Studies law in London: Gandhi trained at the Inner Temple in London and was called to the bar in 1891, before struggling as a lawyer back in India.
Mahatma Gandhi's life, in order.Moves to South Africa: In 1893 he was famously thrown off a train in Pietermaritzburg for refusing to leave a first-class compartment, an experience that shaped him.
Mahatma Gandhi's life, in order.Returns to India: Gandhi returned to India in January 1915 after over twenty years in South Africa, and he soon toured the country by train.
Mahatma Gandhi's life, in order.Salt March: The Salt March ran about 240 miles to Dandi, where Gandhi picked up salt in defiance of the British monopoly.
Mahatma Gandhi's life, in order.Round Table talks in London: During his 1931 visit to London for the talks he stayed in the East End and met workers, and he visited Lancashire textile mills.
Mahatma Gandhi's life, in order.Quit India movement: Do or die was Gandhi's call during the Quit India movement, which prompted the British to jail him and thousands of others.
Mahatma Gandhi's life, in order.India wins independence: India won independence on August 15, 1947, but it came with Partition, which displaced millions and caused terrible violence.
Mahatma Gandhi's life, in order.Assassinated: Nathuram Godse shot Gandhi on January 30, 1948, in Delhi, and the world mourned him as the father of the nation.
